knowledge_point.title: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+6 e^{3 x}=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- 6 e^{3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- 6 e^{3 x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-6\int e^{3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-6\left(\frac{e^{3 x}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=- 2 e^{3 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=6 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=6 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(6 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-6\int - \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-6\left(\frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+3 e^{3 x}=3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=3- 3 e^{3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(3- 3 e^{3 x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=3\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x-3\int e^{3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=3\left(x\right)-3\left(\frac{e^{3 x}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=3 x - e^{3 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)- 2 x^{2}=4 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=4 x+2 x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(4 x+2 x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=4\int x\,\mathrm{d}x+2\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=4\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+2\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=\frac{2 x^{3}}{3} + 2 x^{2}+C \\ &=\frac{2 x^{2} \left(x + 3\right)}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice

question.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=- 7 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int - 7 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-7\int \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-7\left(- 2 \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\right)+C \\  & =C + 14 \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C + 14 \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =14\int \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =14\left(2 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D + 28 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int 4 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4\left(- 2 \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\right)+C \\  & =C - 8 \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C - 8 \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-8\int \cos{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =-8\left(2 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D - 16 \sin{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\left(16 x^{3}\right)=- 2 x^{2}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=8 x^{3} - x^{2}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(8 x^{3} - x^{2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int x^{2}\,\text{d}x + 8\int x^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right) + 8\left(\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right)+C \\  & =C + 2 x^{4} - \frac{x^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C + 2 x^{4} - \frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =- \frac{1}{3}\int x^{3}\,\text{d}x + 2\int x^{4}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =- \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right) + 2\left(\frac{x^{5}}{5}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D + \frac{2 x^{5}}{5} - \frac{x^{4}}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=- 6 x^{2} - 5 x.
$$

Work on a connected interval with $x\ne0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=- 6 x - 5.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(- 6 x - 5\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\int 1\,\text{d}x - 6\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-5\left(x\right) - 6\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\  & =C - 3 x^{2} - 5 x.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C - 3 x^{2} - 5 x\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-5\int x\,\text{d}x - 3\int x^{2}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =-5\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right) - 3\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D - x^{3} - \frac{5 x^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Lengths of the Major and Minor Axes Given the Equation of an Ellipse

question.:question/problem:
For the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{28}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{51}=1,$ find the lengths of its major and minor axes.

$\,$ The length of the major axis is 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ The length of the minor axis is 
{{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=28$ and ${b}^{2}=51.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=28,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{28}=2\sqrt{7}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=51,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{51}.$

Thus, the semi-major axis has length $b=\sqrt{51},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=2\sqrt{7}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot \sqrt{51}=2\sqrt{51},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 2\sqrt{7}=4\sqrt{7}.$

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=2$ and ${b}^{2}=9.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=2,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{2}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=9,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{9}=3.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=3,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 3=6,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}.$

question.:question/problem: A school administrator observed that the growth of the number of students enrolled in a program is directly proportional to the difference between the program’s maximum enrollment capacity and the current number of students enrolled. Let $S(t)$ be the number of students enrolled, measured in students, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in years. If the maximum number of students the program can support is $70$ students, which differential equation could be used to model the number of students enrolled in the program? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate at which the number of students enrolled $S(t)$ in the program changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum number of students the program can support and the current number of students enrolled. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}=k(a-S),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of students the program can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=70\text{ students},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}=k(70-S).
$$

domains.capacity: positive integer; current stock below capacity

question.:question/problem: The rate at which a cup of chocolate cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the chocolate in degrees Celsius, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${19}^{∘}\text{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the chocolate? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Write the equation in terms of the given constant $k$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={19}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-19).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=- \sin{\left(\frac{y}{x} \right)} + \frac{2 y}{x}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- \sin{\left(\frac{y}{x} \right)} + \frac{2 y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =2 v - \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =2 v - \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =v - \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =v - \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ \left(\frac{1}{v - \sin{\left(v \right)}}\right)\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=- 3 \sin{\left(\frac{y}{x} \right)} + \frac{3 y}{x}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 3 \sin{\left(\frac{y}{x} \right)} + \frac{3 y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =3 v - 3 \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =3 v - 3 \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =2 v - 3 \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =2 v - 3 \sin{\left(v \right)} \\ \left(\frac{1}{2 v - 3 \sin{\left(v \right)}}\right)\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{-8x^3+y^3}{xy^2}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{-8x^3+(vx)^3}{x(vx)^2} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{-8+v^3}{v^2}=\frac{-8}{v^2}+v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{-8}{v^2} \\ v^2\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{-8}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v^2\,\mathrm{d}v&=-8\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^3}{3}&=-8\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^3&=-24\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^3&=-24\ln|x|+C \\ y^3&=x^3(-24\ln|x|+C) \\ y&=x\sqrt[3]{-24\ln|x|+C}\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=3C_1$ and the cube root is real. Restrict the solution to intervals where $y\ne0$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x+y}{x}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x+(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=1+v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ v&=\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}&=\ln|x|+C \\ y&=x\ln|x|+Cx\end{aligned}
$$



The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation. Consider the solutions with $y\ne0$.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{yx}{y^2+x^2}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)x}{(vx)^2+x^2} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v}{v^2+1} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v}{v^2+1}-v=-\frac{v^3}{v^2+1} \\ \frac{v^2+1}{v^3}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{v^2+1}{v^3}\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int\left(\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{v^3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ \ln|v|-\frac{1}{2v^2}&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ 2\ln|v|-\frac{1}{v^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C \\ 2\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|+2\ln|x|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=C \\ 2\ln|y|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=C\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The constant solution $y=0$ was excluded by the question; division by $v$ is therefore valid.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^2-4x^2}{xy}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because all terms in the numerator and denominator have degree 2 (quadratic).

With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^2-4x^2}{x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^2-4}{v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^2-4}{v}-v=-\frac{4}{v} \\ v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{4}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\,\mathrm{d}v&=-4\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^2}{2}&=-4\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2&=-8\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=-8\ln|x|+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}&=-4\ln(x^2)+C \\ y^2&=-4x^2\ln(x^2)+Cx^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$; use $2\ln|x|=\ln(x^2)$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\left(6 x + 48\right)\sqrt[3]{y^2}.$ Work on intervals where $y\ne 0$; cube roots are real.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\left(6 x + 48\right)\sqrt[3]{y^2} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{y^2}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =2 x + 16\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{y^2}}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 2 x + 16\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =\left(x + 8\right)^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
\sqrt[3]{y}=\left(x + 8\right)^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ Solving for $y$ gives

$$
y=\left(C + \left(x + 8\right)^{2}\right)^{3}.
$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

$$

$$
y^{3}=\left(x - 3\right)^{2}+C.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}={(x+1)}^{2}y$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(x+1)}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={(x+1)}^{2}y \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={(x+1)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {(x+1)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {(x+1)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {(x+1)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\frac{1}{3}\,{(x+1)}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\frac{1}{3}\,{(x+1)}^{3}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{(x+1)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x+1)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x+1)}^{3}/3}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{{(x+1)}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{{(x+1)}^{3}/3}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+2)}$ for $y\ne 0$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}<(x+2)<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+2)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+2)} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+2)} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={sec}^{2}⁡(x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x+2)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x+2)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x+2)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+2)}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=5 e^{4 x - y}.$ Work on intervals where the logarithm argument is positive.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =5 e^{4 x - y} \\ e^{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =5 e^{4 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int e^{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int 5 e^{4 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int e^{y}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 5 e^{4 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ e^{y} & =\frac{5 e^{4 x}}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
e^{y}=\frac{5 e^{4 x}}{4}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\ln{\left(C + \frac{5 e^{4 x}}{4} \right)}.
$$

The logarithm argument must be positive on the solution interval; $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{3 \left(x - 2\right)^{4}}{y}.$ Assume $x-2>0.$ Take both sign branches on intervals where the radicand is positive and $y\ne 0.$

To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{3 \left(x - 2\right)^{4}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =3 \left(x - 2\right)^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{4}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{4}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =\frac{3 \left(x - 2\right)^{5}}{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\frac{3 \left(x - 2\right)^{5}}{5}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =\frac{6 \left(x - 2\right)^{5}}{5}+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{6 \left(x - 2\right)^{5}}{5}+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{6 \left(x - 2\right)^{5}}{5}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant. Use either sign consistently on each interval where the radicand is positive.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y'-3y=0$ for $y\ne0.$

$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln|y|=3 x+C.

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln|y| & =3 x+C \\ |y| & =e^{3 x+C} \\ |y| & =e^{3 x}\cdot e^C \\ |y| & =K e^{3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=e^C$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K e^{3 x}.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=6y+3y{x}^{2}$ for $y\ne 0.$

To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$

\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|={x}^{3}+6x+C.

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differential equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\cdot \sqrt{3+{y}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\sqrt{y + 5})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\sqrt{x + 2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int (\sqrt{y + 5})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (\sqrt{x + 2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int (\sqrt{y + 5})\,\text{d}y & =\int (\sqrt{x + 2})\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2 \left(y + 5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} & =\frac{2 \left(x + 2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}+K \\ \left(y + 5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} & =\left(x + 2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3}{2}K.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\left(y + 5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=\left(x + 2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\left(y - 2\right) e^{x - 4}$ for $\left(y-2\right)\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\left(y - 2\right) e^{x - 4} \\ \left(\frac{1}{y - 2}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{x - 4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \left(\frac{1}{y - 2}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (e^{x - 4})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \left(\frac{1}{y - 2}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (e^{x - 4})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \left(\frac{1}{y - 2}\right)\,\text{d}y & =\int (e^{x - 4})\,\text{d}x \\ \ln{\left(\left|{y - 2}\right| \right)} & =e^{x - 4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln{\left(\left|{y - 2}\right| \right)}=e^{x - 4}+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2 e^{2 x - y} - e^{- y}.$ **Hint:** Factor the common exponential before separating the variables.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Factor $e^{-y}$ from the right-hand side, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 e^{2 x - y} - e^{- y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{-y}(2 e^{2 x} - 1) \\ (e^{y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 e^{2 x} - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate both sides term by term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y})\,\text{d}y & =\int (2 e^{2 x} - 1)\,\text{d}x \\ e^{y} & =- x + e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
e^{y}=- x + e^{2 x}+C.
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- e^{x - y} + e^{- y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{-y}(1 - e^{x}) \\ (e^{y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 - e^{x}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Given that $f(x)=\left(- 4 x - 3\right)^{4}$, find $f^{\prime}(x).$

Use the decomposition $g(x)=- 4 x - 3$ and $F(u)=u^{4}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$. Recall that $f^{\prime}(x)=F^{\prime}(g(x))g^{\prime}(x)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $g(x)=- 4 x - 3$ and $F(g)=g^{4}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$.

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} F^{\prime}(g)&=4 g^{3}, \\ g^{\prime}(x)&=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule,

$$
\begin{aligned} f^{\prime}(x)&=F^{\prime}(g(x))\cdot g^{\prime}(x) \\ &=\left(4 \left(- 4 x - 3\right)^{3}\right)\cdot\left(-4\right) \\ &=- 16 \left(- 4 x - 3\right)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Identifying Inhibited Growth Equations and Initial Value Problems

question.:question/problem: Given that $y<110$ and $t\ge 0$, which of the following is an inhibited growth equation throughout this range?
question.:question/worked-solution:
An inhibited growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=k(a-y),\qquad k>0.
$$

The quantity must be below its equilibrium: $y<a$.

The matching choice is

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=2(110-y).
$$



The equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}&=-10(y-60) \\ &=10(60-y) \\ a&=60\end{aligned}
$$

The equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}&=2(110-y) \\ a&=110\end{aligned}
$$

The equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}&=-2(y+110) \\ a&=-110\end{aligned}
$$

The choice $\frac{dy}{dt}=-2(110-y)$ has a positive linear coefficient, so its rate is not a positive constant times the remaining gap.

question.:question/problem:
The temperature of a drink $P(t)$, measured in degrees Celsius, obeys

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(31-P),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is measured in minutes and $k>0$ is constant. At $t=0$, the quantity is $8$ degrees Celsius. At $t=3$, it is $17$ degrees Celsius. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $28$ degrees Celsius? Round to the nearest integer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(31-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{31-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|31-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}31-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=31-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the initial condition:

$$
K=31-8=23.
$$

Calibrate the rate with the later observation:

$$
\begin{aligned}23e^{-3k}&=14 \\ -3k&=\ln\left(\frac{14}{23}\right) \\ k&=\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{23}{14}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
P(t)=31-23e^{-kt}.
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3&=23e^{-k(t-0)} \\ -k(t-0)&=\ln\left(\frac{3}{23}\right) \\ t&=0+\frac{\ln\left(\frac{23}{3}\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 12.309008 \\ &\approx 12.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $12$ minutes from the start of monitoring.

knowledge_point.title: Identifying Homogeneous Differential Equations

question.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $1$, so a factor $t^{1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=t\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-3\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $2$, so a factor $t^{2}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{2}\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-3\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x\,\left(x + \left(-3\right)\,y\right)}{x\,\left(x + 3\,y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. Numerator and denominator have the same total degree $2$. Their scaling factors cancel.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{t\,x\,\left(t\,x + \left(-3\right)\,t\,y\right)}{t\,x\,\left(t\,x + 3\,t\,y\right)}\\ &=\frac{x\,\left(x + \left(-3\right)\,y\right)}{x\,\left(x + 3\,y\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-1\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $2$, so a factor $t^{2}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{2}\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-1\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}{y\,\left(x + y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $1$, so a factor $t^{1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=t\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}{y\,\left(x + y\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=6$ and the vertical radius has length $b=1.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{1} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Linear Exponent

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=6{e}^{u}-4,\,u=-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=6{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =6{e}^{u}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-24{e}^{u} \\  & =-24{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=-2{e}^{-4x}$ at the point where $x=- \frac{1}{4}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-2{e}^{u},\,u=-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-2{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-2{e}^{u}\cdot (-4) \\  & =8{e}^{u} \\  & =8{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=- \frac{1}{4}$, evaluate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}m &= 8{e}^{-4x}\big|_{x=- \frac{1}{4}} \\ &= 8{e}^{(-4)\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)} \\ &= 8 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}y_1 &= -2{e}^{-4x}\big|_{x=- \frac{1}{4}} \\ &= -2{e}^{(-4)\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)} \\ &= - 2 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 &=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(- 2 e) &= (8 e)(x-\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)) \\ y-(- 2 e) &= 8 e x-(- 2 e) \\ y &= 8 e x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve $y={3}^{3x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{3}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={3}^{u},\,u=3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={3}^{u}\ln(3),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={3}^{u}\ln(3)\cdot (3) \\ & =(3)\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3) \\ & =3\cdot {3}^{3x}\ln(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{3}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=\frac{1}{3}} & =(3)\cdot {3}^{3\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}\ln(3) \\ & =3\cdot {3}^{1}\ln(3) \\ & =9 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{3}$ is $9 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.$

question.:question/problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of a fresh-baked cake can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.16(T-76)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the cake is ${367}^{∘}F,$ calculate the temperature of the cake after $6$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fresh-baked cake is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.16(T-76).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-76} & =-0.16\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-76} & =-\int 0.16\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-76| & =-0.16t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-76>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-76 & ={e}^{-0.16t+C} \\ T-76 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T-76 & =K{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T & =76+K{e}^{-0.16t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the cake was ${367}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=367,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}367 & =76+K{e}^{0} \\ 367 & =76+K \\ K & =291\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=76+291{e}^{-0.16t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the cake after $t=6$ minutes is

$$
T(6)=76+291{e}^{-0.16\cdot 6}≈{187}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.:question/problem:
The water boils in a pan at a temperature of ${100}^{∘}C.$ The pan with water is then placed to a room with a temperature of ${26}^{∘}C,$ and the temperature of water decreases. After $5$ minutes, it cools to ${93}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the water to have a temperature of ${56}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the water in the pan decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the water starts cooling.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={26}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-26).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-26} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-26} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-26| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-26>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-26 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-26 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-26 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =26+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature was ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=100,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =26+K{e}^{0} \\ 100 & =26+K \\ K & =74\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=26+74{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $5$ minutes, it cools to ${93}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(5)=93,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}93 & =26+74{e}^{-5k} \\ 67 & =74{e}^{-5k} \\ \frac{67}{74} & ={e}^{-5k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{67}{74}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{67}{74}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the water has a temperature of ${56}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =56 \\ 26+74{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =56 \\ 74{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =30 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{15}{37} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{15}{37}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{15}{37}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the temperature of water will be ${56}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{15}{37}\right)}{-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{67}{74}\right)}≈45\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

We're told that the initial temperature of the pork leg was ${127}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=127,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}127 & =31+K{e}^{0} \\ 127 & =31+K \\ K & =96\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T(t)=31+96{e}^{-kt}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}51 & =31+96{e}^{-3k} \\ 20 & =96{e}^{-3k} \\ \frac{5}{24} & ={e}^{-3k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{24}\right) & =-3k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{24}\right)\end{aligned}

$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the pork leg will have a temperature of ${35}^{∘}C$ after

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${88}^{∘}C.$ After $8$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${51}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${35}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${25}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={25}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-25).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-25} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-25} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-25| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-25>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-25 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-25 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-25 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =25+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${88}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=88,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}88 & =25+K{e}^{0} \\ 88 & =25+K \\ K & =63\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=25+63{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $8$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${51}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(8)=51,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}51 & =25+63{e}^{-8k} \\ 26 & =63{e}^{-8k} \\ \frac{26}{63} & ={e}^{-8k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{26}{63}\right) & =-8k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{26}{63}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${35}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =35 \\ 25+63{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =35 \\ 63{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =10 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{10}{63} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{10}{63}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{10}{63}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${35}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{10}{63}\right)}{-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{26}{63}\right)}≈17\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${26}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${124}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $3$ minutes and ${86}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $9$ minutes. The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, obeys Newton's law of cooling, with $t$ measured in minutes since cooling began. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${35}^{∘}\text{C}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-26),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-26} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-26} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-26| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-26>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-26 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-26 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-26 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =26+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(3)=124$ and $T(9)=86$:

$$
\begin{aligned}124 & =26+Ke^{-3k} \\ 98 & =Ke^{-3k} \\ 86 & =26+Ke^{-9k} \\ 60 & =Ke^{-9k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{60}{98} & =\frac{Ke^{-9k}}{Ke^{-3k}} \\ \frac{30}{49} & =e^{-6k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{30}{49}\right) & =-6k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(3)=124$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}98 & =Ke^{-3\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)} \\ K & =98e^{3\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)} \\ K & =98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=26+98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3) & =26+(98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)\cdot 3}=124 \\ T(9) & =26+(98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)\cdot 9}=86\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${35}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =35 \\ 26+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =35 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =9 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{9}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{9}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{9}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}}\ln\left(\frac{9}{98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =3+6\frac{\ln\left(\frac{9}{98}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{30}{49}\right)}≈32\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+8 x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- 8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- 8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 x^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 8 e^{2 x}=8 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} &=8 e^{2 x}+8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 e^{2 x}+8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ y &=8\int e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=4 x^{2} + 4 e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}.$

First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}.$

First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int \frac{1}{2 x - 2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{\ln{\left(\left|{2 x - 2}\right| \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 \ln{\left(\left|{2 x - 2}\right| \right)}+C\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)- 8 x^{2}=8 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8 x+8 x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 x+8 x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=\frac{8 x^{3}}{3} + 4 x^{2}+C \\ &=\frac{4 x^{2} \left(2 x + 3\right)}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=-7.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int -7\,\text{d}x \\  & =-7\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-7\left(x\right)+C \\  & =C - 7 x.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C - 7 x\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-7\int x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =-7\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D - \frac{7 x^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C + 3 x^{2} + 8 x\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =8\int x\,\text{d}x + 3\int x^{2}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right) + 3\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D + x^{3} + 4 x^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{5}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=5$ and ${b}^{2}=4.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=5,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{5}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=4,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{4}=2.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=\sqrt{5},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=2.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{5}=2\sqrt{5},$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2=4.$

question.:question/problem: A factory's management noted that the growth of the unit production is directly proportional to the difference between the maximum number of units a factory worker can produce and the current production quantity. Let $P(t)$ be the production quantity, measured in units produced, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in days. If the maximum number of units that a worker can produce is $410$ $\text{units}$, which differential equation could be used to model the factory's production? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate at which the production $P(t)$ of the factory changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum number of units a factory worker can produce and the current production quantity. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of units a factory worker can produce, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=410\text{ units},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=k(410-P).
$$

question.:question/problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of an exhaust pipe of a motorcycle can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.04(T-71)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe is ${205}^{∘}F,$ calculate its temperature after $3$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.04(T-71).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-71} & =-0.04\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-71} & =-\int 0.04\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-71| & =-0.04t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-71>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-71 & ={e}^{-0.04t+C} \\ T-71 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.04t} \\ T-71 & =K{e}^{-0.04t} \\ T & =71+K{e}^{-0.04t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${205}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=205,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}205 & =71+K{e}^{0} \\ 205 & =71+K \\ K & =134\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=71+134{e}^{-0.04t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=71+134{e}^{-0.04\cdot 3}≈{190}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${21}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${103}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $1$ minute and ${52}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $3$ minutes. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${23}^{∘}\text{C}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-21),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-21} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-21} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-21| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-21>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-21 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-21 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-21 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =21+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(1)=103$ and $T(3)=52$:

$$
\begin{aligned}103 & =21+Ke^{-1k} \\ 82 & =Ke^{-1k} \\ 52 & =21+Ke^{-3k} \\ 31 & =Ke^{-3k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{31}{82} & =\frac{Ke^{-3k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{31}{82} & =e^{-2k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{31}{82}\right) & =-2k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=103$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}82 & =Ke^{-1\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)} \\ K & =82e^{1\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)} \\ K & =82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=21+82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)t}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =21+(82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)\cdot 1}=103 \\ T(3) & =21+(82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)\cdot 3}=52\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}}\ln\left(\frac{2}{82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =1+2\frac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{41}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{31}{82}\right)}≈9\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5x-1}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=5x-1.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (5) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{(5x-1{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{1-4x}$ at the point where $x=-2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=1-4x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-2} & ={\left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x}}\right)|}_{x=-2} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2\sqrt{1-4(-2)}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2\sqrt{9}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+12x.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+12.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (6x+12) \\  & =-\frac{6x+12}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}+12x{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={\left(-\frac{6x+12}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}+12x{)}^{3}}}\right)|}_{x=2} \\  & =-\frac{6(2)+12}{2\sqrt{(3(2{)}^{2}+12(2){)}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{24}{2\sqrt{{36}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Let $u=x-3.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\left(4 - 4 x\right) e^{- y - 4} \\ (e^{y + 4})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 - 4 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y + 4})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4 - 4 x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (e^{y + 4})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (4 - 4 x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (e^{y + 4})\,\text{d}y & =\int (4 - 4 x)\,\text{d}x \\ e^{y + 4} & =- 2 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
e^{y + 4}=- 2 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}+C.
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=e^{x - y} - 2 e^{- y}.$ **Hint:** Factor the common exponential before separating the variables.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Factor $e^{-y}$ from the right-hand side, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{x - y} - 2 e^{- y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{-y}(e^{x} - 2) \\ (e^{y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{x} - 2\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate both sides term by term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y})\,\text{d}y & =\int (e^{x} - 2)\,\text{d}x \\ e^{y} & =- 2 x + e^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
e^{y}=- 2 x + e^{x}+C.
$$

recipes: integrate x as 1, or 1 as x

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{- y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=- 2 x e^{- y} + e^{x - y}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Collect the derivative terms, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}(1 + e^{- y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x e^{- y} + e^{x - y} \\ (e^{y} + 1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x + e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate both sides term by term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y} + 1)\,\text{d}y & =\int (- 2 x + e^{x})\,\text{d}x \\ y + e^{y} & =- x^{2} + e^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
y + e^{y}=- x^{2} + e^{x}+C.
$$

recipes: integrate x as 1, or 1 as x

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhibited Growth Model

question.:question/problem:
The number of students affected by flu $P(t)$ increases toward a maximum of $1500$ students. Time $t\ge 0$ is measured in days from the start of monitoring. At $t=0$, the quantity is $300$ students. At $t=10$, it is $500$ students. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $800$ students? Round to the nearest integer.

*Hint: Assume an inhibited growth model.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(1500-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{1500-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|1500-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1500-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=1500-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the initial condition:

$$
K=1500-300=1200.
$$

Calibrate the rate with the later observation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1200e^{-10k}&=1000 \\ -10k&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \\ k&=\frac{1}{10}\ln\left(\frac{6}{5}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
P(t)=1500-1200e^{-kt}.
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}700&=1200e^{-k(t-0)} \\ -k(t-0)&=\ln\left(\frac{7}{12}\right) \\ t&=0+\frac{\ln\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 29.562961 \\ &\approx 30.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $30$ days from the start of monitoring.

question.:question/problem:
The daily egg production $P(t)$ increases toward a maximum of $500$ eggs per day. Time $t\ge 0$ is measured in days from the start of monitoring. At $t=3$, the quantity is $390$ eggs per day. At $t=6$, it is $400$ eggs per day. What is the quantity at $t=42$? Round to the nearest integer.

*Hint: Assume an inhibited growth model.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(500-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{500-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|500-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}500-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=500-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two observations give two deficit equations. Dividing eliminates $K$:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ke^{-3k}&=110 \\ Ke^{-6k}&=100 \\ e^{3k}&=\frac{11}{10} \\ k&=\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{11}{10}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute back for the integration constant and combine the exponentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}K&=110e^{3k} \\ P(t)&=500-110e^{3k}e^{-kt} \\ &=500-110e^{-k(t-3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate using the exact rate, keeping full precision until the final step:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(42)&=500-110e^{-k(42-3)} \\ &\approx 468.136918 \\ &\approx 468.\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity is approximately $468$ eggs per day.

question.:question/problem:
The temperature of a drink $P(t)$, measured in degrees Celsius, obeys

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(20-P),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is measured in minutes and $k>0$ is constant. At $t=0$, the quantity is $8$ degrees Celsius. At $t=5$, it is $12$ degrees Celsius. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $16$ degrees Celsius? Round to the nearest integer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(20-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{20-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|20-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}20-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=20-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the initial condition:

$$
K=20-8=12.
$$

Calibrate the rate with the later observation:

$$
\begin{aligned}12e^{-5k}&=8 \\ -5k&=\ln\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \\ k&=\frac{1}{5}\ln\left(\frac{3}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
P(t)=20-12e^{-kt}.
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}4&=12e^{-k(t-0)} \\ -k(t-0)&=\ln\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\ t&=0+\frac{\ln\left(3\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 13.547556 \\ &\approx 14.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $14$ minutes from the start of monitoring.

question.:question/problem: Which of the following initial value problems is an inhibited decay problem?
question.:question/worked-solution:
An inhibited decay initial value problem has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-k(y-a),\,y(0)={y}_{0}
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $y>a$ for all $t>0.$

From the given options, the only inhibited decay problem is

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-2(y-500),\,y(0)=600.
$$

In this case, $k=2,a=500,$ and ${y}_{0}=600.$ Notice that ${y}_{0}>a,$ which is required for inhibited decay. 

The other options do not represent inhibited decay. In particular, the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-2(y-500),\,y(0)=400,
$$

does *not* represent inhibited decay model because ${y}_{0}=400<a=500.$

generation.sampling_policy: positive integer equilibrium; equation integer rates; IVP exact terminating rates and 0<below<a<above

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y={e}^{7+3x}$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u=7+3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 3 \\  & =3{e}^{u} \\  & =3{e}^{7+3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the sum rule of differentiation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}+{e}^{7+3x}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+(3{e}^{7+3x}) \\  & =3({x}^{2}+{e}^{7+3x}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=-5{e}^{-3x}$ at the point where $x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-5{e}^{u},\,u=-3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-5{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-5{e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =15{e}^{u} \\  & =15{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$, evaluate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}m &= 15{e}^{-3x}\big|_{x=0} \\ &= 15{e}^{(-3)(0)} \\ &= 15.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}y_1 &= -5{e}^{-3x}\big|_{x=0} \\ &= -5{e}^{(-3)(0)} \\ &= -5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 &=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(-5) &= (15)(x-(0)) \\ y-(-5) &= 15 x-(0) \\ y &= 15 x - 5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+6 e^{- 3 x}=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=1- 6 e^{- 3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(1- 6 e^{- 3 x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=1\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x-6\int e^{- 3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=1\left(x\right)-6\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=x + 2 e^{- 3 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=3 \cdot 2^{x} - 4 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(3 \cdot 2^{x} - 4 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int 2^{x}\,\text{d}x - 4\int \sin{\left(3 x \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3\left(\frac{2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\right) - 4\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\right)+C \\  & =\frac{3 \cdot 2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}} + C + \frac{4 \cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{3 \cdot 2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}} + C + \frac{4 \cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{3}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\int 2^{x}\,\text{d}x  \\ &\quad + \frac{4}{3}\int \cos{\left(3 x \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ &\quad +C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(\frac{2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\right)  \\ &\quad + \frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{\sin{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\right) \\ &\quad +Cx \\ &\quad +D \\  & =\frac{3 \cdot 2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2}} + C x + D + \frac{4 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.:question/problem:
For the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{81}=1,$ find the lengths of its major and minor axes.

$\,$ The length of the major axis is 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ The length of the minor axis is 
{{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=16$ and ${b}^{2}=81.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=16,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{16}=4.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=81,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{81}=9.$

Thus, the semi-major axis has length $b=9,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=4.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 9=18,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 4=8.$

question.:question/problem: The growth of the number of animals in a rehabilitation aquarium is directly proportional to the difference between its maximum capacity and its current population. Let $M(t)$ be the number of animals, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in months. If the maximum capacity is $85$ animals, which differential equation models this population? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the current quantity. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=k(a-M),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity and $k>0$.

Here $a=85$, so

$$
\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=k(85-M).
$$

question.:question/problem:
A thermometer is placed into a water bath and displays a reading of ${78}^{∘}C.$ The thermometer is then transferred to a ${12}^{∘}C$ water bath, and its reading begins to decrease. After $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the thermometer to register a reading of ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred into the ${12}^{∘}C$ water bath.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${78}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=78,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}78 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 78 & =12+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+66{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(12)=58,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}58 & =12+66{e}^{-12k} \\ 46 & =66{e}^{-12k} \\ \frac{23}{33} & ={e}^{-12k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right) & =-12k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the thermometer reads ${28}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =28 \\ 12+66{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =28 \\ 66{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =16 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{8}{33} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the thermometer will read ${28}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right)}{-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right)}≈47\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

$$
\begin{aligned}T-17 & ={e}^{-0.16t+C} \\ T-17 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T-17 & =K{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T & =17+K{e}^{-0.16t}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
